parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бу́лочка (búločka) and Ukrainian бу́лочка (búločka).

parole.significato: The name of the letter м/М in Cyrillic alphabets.
parole.testo: From Russian эм (em), Ukrainian ем (em), etc.

parole.significato: The head of a group or unit of Cossacks.
parole.testo: From Russian есау́л (jesaúl), Ukrainian осаву́л (osavúl). Ultimately from Middle Mongol 札撒兀勒 (zhásāwùlè /⁠⁠ǰasa'ul⁠/).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Russian-Empire writer Nikolai Gogol (1809–1852) or his works.
parole.testo: From Gogol + -ian, from Russian Го́голь (Gógolʹ) and Ukrainian Го́голь (Hóholʹ) from Ukrainian го́голь (hóholʹ, “common goldeneye, Bucephala clangula”), from Old East Slavic гоголь (gogolĭ) < Proto-Slavic *gogolĭ.

parole.significato: A guided bomb (GBU), in a Soviet or post-Soviet (especially Russian or Ukrainian) military context.
parole.testo: From Russian КАБ (KAB) or sometimes Ukrainian КАБ (KAB), from Russian корректируемых авиационных бомб (korrektirujemyx aviacionnyx bomb) and Ukrainian корегованих авіаційних бомб (korehovanyx aviacijnyx bomb).

parole.significato: A pork jelly or aspic traditionally eaten in Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine.
parole.testo: From Russian холоде́ц (xolodéc) or Ukrainian холоде́ць (xolodécʹ), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xolditi.

parole.significato: A large, single-piece round or rectangular loaf of bread, elaborately decorated and served at a wedding
parole.testo: From older Russian корова́й (korováj) (before 1956 reform) or Ukrainian корова́й (korováj). The modern Russian spelling is карава́й (karaváj).

parole.significato: A ceremonial grain dish with sweet gravy traditionally served mostly by Eastern Orthodox Christians and some Catholic C…
parole.testo: From Russian кутья (kutʹja) and Ukrainian кутя (kutja).

parole.testo: From Russian лима́н (limán) or Ukrainian лима́н (lymán), from Turkic, compare Turkish liman (“port, harbor”). Ultimately from Ancient Greek λιμήν (limḗn, “harbor”).
Semantic loan from Russian па́блик (páblik) and Ukrainian па́блік (páblik, “public webpage on a blog or on social media”), both borrowed from English public: see etymology 1.

parole.significato: a semi-official designation for a settlement with a rural character, where settlement would not be enough to distinguis…
parole.testo: Calque of Russian посёлок се́льского ти́па (posjólok sélʹskovo típa), Ukrainian се́лище сільсько́го ти́пу (sélyšče silʹsʹkóho týpu), or similar.

parole.significato: a type of fatback, or non-rendered underskin pig fat consumed in Central and Eastern Europe, usually seasoned
parole.testo: From Russian са́ло (sálo) or Ukrainian са́ло (sálo), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sadlo.
Calque of Russian сингармони́зм (singarmonízm), Ukrainian сингармоні́зм (synharmonízm).

parole.significato: A horse-drawn machine gun, usually a cart or open wagon with the gun installed in the back.
parole.testo: From Russian тачанка (tačanka) or Ukrainian тачанка (tačanka).

parole.significato: To render Ukrainian in character; impose Ukrainian culture, language, or ethnic identity.
parole.testo: 1915, Ukrainian + -ize. The shorter form, cognate of Ukrainization/Ukrainisation is influenced by Russian украиниза́ция (ukrainizácija) or Ukrainian україніза́ція (ukrajinizácija).

parole.significato: freedom; lack of restraint or constriction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian во́ля (vólja) or Ukrainian во́ля (vólja).

parole.significato: A traditional administrative subdivision in Eastern Europe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian во́лость (vólostʹ) and Ukrainian во́лость (vólostʹ), from Old East Slavic волость (volostĭ).
